items.title: An Alabama coal mine gives up North America's oldest modern-lineage scorpion
items.why: Not a dinosaur, but the palaeontology desk takes what the Carboniferous sends, and this one predates the first dinosaurs by around 80 million years. Worth noticing that the find comes from a working coal mine, which is to say the scorpion's swamp eventually became somebody's fuel.
items.summary: Palaeontologists from Flinders University, the American Museum of Natural History and the University of Alabama describe a scorpion from roughly 316 to 319 million years ago, found in an Alabama coal mine. They say it is the oldest known member of the modern scorpion lineage in North America.

items.title: Verica, the British ruler whose exile invited the Roman invasion, may have been a woman
items.why: History class gives Claudius a tidy pretext for invading Britain in AD 43: a deposed client king turns up in Rome asking for help. If the new reading holds, that king was a queen, and the textbooks have had the pronoun wrong for two thousand years. The place is very much the point here, so it goes under UK rather than archaeology at large.
items.summary: Archaeologists report evidence that Verica, the Iron Age ruler in southern Britain whose flight to Rome helped set off the Roman conquest, was a woman rather than a man. If accepted, it would recast a pivotal figure in early British history as a largely forgotten female leader.

items.title: The oldest known close pair of quasars, already enormous 900 million years after the Big Bang
items.why: Supermassive black holes that arrive early keep embarrassing the growth models, and here are two of them in a tight pair. One weighs about 1.5 billion suns and the other about 400 million, which is a lot of mass to assemble before the universe was a billion years old.
items.summary: Astronomers have found the most ancient compact quasar pair yet, seen as it was roughly 900 million years after the Big Bang. The two black holes powering it are about 1.5 billion and 400 million solar masses, larger than current theories comfortably allow at that age.

items.title: Down to the last 50: what it took for species like the Mauritius kestrel to come back
items.why: In 1974 there were four Mauritius kestrels left in the wild, and a respected environmentalist argued the money would be better spent elsewhere. Conservationists ignored him, and the bird is now the poster raptor for a study of 141 species pushed below 50 animals. The headline finding is calm rather than grim: recovery happens, but almost never on its own.
items.summary: A study in the Proceedings of the Royal Society B, led by Donal Smith at Monash University, looked at 141 bird and mammal species whose wild numbers fell below 50. Many recovered, but nearly always with active help such as captive breeding, predator control and releases; the Mauritius kestrel climbed from four birds into the hundreds, though it has slipped again since.

items.title: Estes Park's Tower of Love, a theatre spire built for a romance that fell through
items.why: Most monuments to love celebrate a happy ending; this one marks a man left at the altar who answered by bolting a glowing tower onto his cinema. The coda is the best part: when a sign ordinance came for the neon, the town voted to keep it lit.
items.summary: The Historic Park Theatre in Estes Park, Colorado, dates to 1913, and its tower was added by owner Ralph Gwynn in 1929. Local legend says he built it after being jilted, and residents later won a ballot measure exempting its neon outline from a new sign rule.

items.title: A Pokemon Red romhack where every playground rumour is finally true
items.why: Anyone who spent a recess in 1999 arguing about the truck near the S.S. Anne will understand the appeal. The author built on the community disassembly of the original game and ships a patcher rather than a ROM, which is the polite, old-fashioned way to do it. Getting to the truck is still as fiddly as it ever was, on purpose.
items.summary: A hobbyist has made a romhack of the first-generation Pokemon games that implements the most famous schoolyard urban legends, including Mew hiding under the truck. It is distributed as a browser-based patcher you apply to your own ROM, with the source published, and builds on the open reverse-engineering project for the original game.

items.title: La Mettrie's Man a Machine, the 18th-century book that got its author run out of town
items.why: La Mettrie argued in the 1740s that the mind is just what the body's machinery does, which got him chased out of France and then the Netherlands before Frederick the Great took him in. The Public Domain Review has the 1749 English edition, and it reads like a very early draft of an argument cognitive science is still having.
items.summary: The Public Domain Review presents the 1749 English edition of Man a Machine by the French physician-philosopher Julien Offray de La Mettrie. The book makes a thoroughgoing materialist case that thought arises from the body, and La Mettrie is now often counted as a forefather of cognitive science.

items.title: How a mechanical watch keeps time, with parts you can spin around
items.why: A gentle, interactive walk through hairspring, balance and escapement, with 3D figures you can drag. The author pitches it as an on-ramp to Bartosz Ciechanowski's famously exhaustive watch page, which is a fair description and a fine reason to read both. Notice how much of the design dates back to cathedral clocks.
items.summary: An illustrated explainer of how a modern mechanical watch works, starting from Huygens's 1675 hairspring and building up through the parts that count and release each beat. The rotatable 3D drawings work on a phone too, and it is meant as a simpler introduction before deeper treatments.

items.title: Nightmare mode: injecting the full menu of disk failures into a deterministic simulator
items.why: It comes from a testing vendor's blog, so salt accordingly, but the substance is the familiar catalogue of storage pain: failed writes that may or may not be retryable, full disks forcing compaction, inode exhaustion, and the rename-over trick everyone relies on. Anyone who has chased a durability bug through a filesystem will recognise each case before the authors name it.
items.summary: Antithesis engineers describe a mode in their deterministic simulation environment that injects realistic storage faults into the systems under test. The post walks through why reliable storage is hard even on good days, and how errors like out-of-space, out-of-inodes and failed writes force decisions about retrying, compacting or giving up.

items.title: Fan artist Jeanne Gomoll wins a Moth GrandSLAM with 'Barbie's Inferno'
items.why: Jeanne Gomoll has been a fixture of Madison fandom and its fanzines for decades, so it is pleasing to see her take a storytelling crown on a home-town stage. Small news, but the kind fandom does best: one of its own doing well somewhere unexpected.
items.summary: Longtime science fiction fan writer and artist Jeanne Gomoll won The Moth GrandSLAM storytelling contest with a story called 'Barbie's Inferno', told live at the Barrymore Theater in Madison, Wisconsin, in early October.

items.title: A 67-million-year-old T. rex is heading for its UK public debut in Portsmouth
items.why: Britain has had plenty of plaster casts, but a genuine Tyrannosaurus going on public show is rare enough to count as news, and this announcement comes straight from the university hosting it. Dinosaur news always makes the cut, and this one comes with a road-trip angle for anyone in England this winter.
items.summary: The University of Portsmouth says a Tyrannosaurus rex specimen dated to around 67 million years ago will go on public display in the city, billed as the animal's first public appearance in the UK. Details of the exhibition and the specimen are in the university's announcement.

items.title: Neutron scans reveal a tiny horned reptile from 156 million years ago
items.why: Not a dinosaur, strictly, but a pocket-sized horned reptile from the Late Jurassic counts as palaeontology news by any reasonable editor's standard. The neutron imaging is the clever part, since neutrons can see into fossil-bearing rock in ways X-rays struggle with, and the headline promises a death metal connection, which is more than most species descriptions offer.
items.summary: Researchers used neutron scanning to examine a small fossil reptile about 156 million years old and describe it as a new species with horn-like features, nicknamed a tiny prehistoric dragon. The story also involves death metal, though how is best left to the article.

items.title: Webb maps the hot dust of Cassiopeia A
items.why: Cas A is the supernova remnant everyone has a favourite picture of, and Webb's mid-infrared view adds another worth keeping. The interesting bit is forensic: the mix of elements in the dust is a clue to how the original star was layered before it blew.
items.summary: NASA released a James Webb Space Telescope image of Cassiopeia A in the mid-infrared, showing the warm dust spread through the remnant. Astronomers use the dust's composition to reconstruct the structure of the massive star that exploded.

items.title: Why avian botulism strikes in warm, shallow, green water
items.why: Less cheerful than a raptor portrait, but useful knowledge for anyone who spends mornings at wetlands with binoculars. It reads as a calm explainer of the conditions that set up outbreaks, which is the sort of thing that helps a birder notice when a favourite marsh is starting to look wrong.
items.summary: A 10,000 Birds piece explains why avian botulism outbreaks cluster in warm, shallow, nutrient-rich wetlands. It draws on research from Great Salt Lake, Spain and Miami to link water quality changes with the risk of die-offs among waterbirds.

items.title: The Morning Paper revisits Pregel, Google's graph-processing system
items.why: A trip back to 2010 and the paper that taught a generation to think like a vertex. Adrian Colyer's write-up is a good reminder of how much of later graph and dataflow work descends from Pregel's bulk synchronous supersteps, message passing and checkpoint-based fault tolerance.
items.summary: An archive post from The Morning Paper walks through Pregel, Google's system for processing graphs with billions of vertices and edges. It covers the vertex-centric programming model, the superstep structure borrowed from bulk synchronous parallel computing, and how the system handles scale and failures.

items.title: FRSTPM, the 80287 instruction that apparently does nothing useful
items.why: OS/2 Museum chases down an instruction most people never knew existed, which is precisely the kind of archaeology this feed is for. The trail runs through FSETPM and the 8087's habit of tracking real-mode linear addresses, so expect segment arithmetic and protected-mode history rather than a gentle primer.
items.summary: A reader's question prompts a look at FRSTPM, a documented but obscure instruction found on the 80287XL and M80287 coprocessors but not the original 80287. The piece starts with its sibling FSETPM, which told the coprocessor about protected mode, and works out what FRSTPM was meant to undo.

items.title: A real 1950s telephone switchboard becomes a hotel-operator game
items.why: Someone took an actual Western Electric switchboard and turned it into a game, which is the hobbyist spirit in its purest form: no market, no pitch, just patch cords and joy. Bonus points for a genre nobody knew was missing.
items.summary: Hackaday covers a project built around a genuine 1950s Western Electric switchboard. The player acts as a hotel operator, plugging cords to route incoming calls between guests and the outside world as the game feeds them requests.

items.title: A 1917 cartoon warning America about the perils of the metric system
items.why: More than a century on, the scare tactics look charming, and the United States still measures things in feet, so perhaps the cartoon worked. The Public Domain Review has dug up a fine bit of measurement-war propaganda.
items.summary: The Public Domain Review shares an American cartoon from 1917 that depicts the supposedly dire consequences of adopting the metric system. It comes from a period when a push for metric conversion in the US met organised resistance.

items.title: El Vagamundos, the bronze traveller who never leaves Madrid's airport
items.why: Airport art is usually wallpaper, but this one has picked up its own folklore, which is the Atlas Obscura sweet spot. Worth a detour for anyone with a layover in Madrid and a fondness for odd public sculpture.
items.summary: In Terminal 1 of Madrid-Barajas Airport sits a 1996 bronze by Casto Solano of a seated man apparently waiting for a flight. Called El Vagamundos, or The Wanderer, it has gathered stories among travellers and staff about who he is and why he never boards.

items.title: Revisiting David Weber's Mutineer's Moon, where the Moon is a spaceship
items.why: Weber's debut series opener has one of the great pulp premises: the Moon is a disguised warship, and its computer has been waiting a long time. Alan Brown's classic-SF column gives it a fair rereading, affection and creaky bits alike.
items.summary: Reactor's Front Lines and Frontiers column looks back at Mutineer's Moon, the 1991 novel that opens David Weber's Dahak series. The review covers the book's twist-laden premise of a hidden starship and its crew, and how the adventure holds up today.

items.title: A century-old fossil in a museum drawer turns out to be Europe's first megaraptor
items.why: Megaraptors are the big-thumbed hunters of the southern continents, so finding one in an English collection is a bit like discovering a kangaroo in the Domesday Book. The bones sat unrecognised for about a hundred years, which is the usual reminder that the best fieldwork sometimes happens with a torch and a catalogue. Dinosaur news, so it was never not going in.
items.summary: UCL researchers have re-examined a fossil held in a British collection for roughly a century and identified it as a new long-clawed predatory dinosaur. They place it among the megaraptorans, a group otherwise known mostly from South America and Australia, making it the first of its kind recognised in Europe.

items.title: Far-side Moon rocks suggest the early Solar System's bombardment tapered off rather than peaked
items.why: The 'late heavy bombardment', a sudden spike of impacts long after the planets formed, has been in textbooks since the Apollo samples, and has had a wobbly few decades. Samples from the Moon's far side, the half Apollo never touched, now point to a slow decline instead of one big storm. Notice how much a different sampling site can do to a story built on one hemisphere.
items.summary: Researchers dating ancient rocks returned from the lunar far side found impact ages that don't cluster into a single catastrophic episode. Their results suggest asteroid strikes fell off gradually over billions of years, which changes the picture of conditions on the early Earth when life was getting started.

items.title: Wild kiwi roam the hills around Wellington for the first time in 150 years
items.why: Reintroducing a ground-dwelling, nocturnal bird next to a capital city sounds like a dare, and the trick turned out to be years of predator trapping across private land rather than one fenced sanctuary. More than 250 birds in, the Capital Kiwi project has kiwi calling within earshot of the suburbs. A calm, good-news story with a podcast attached.
items.summary: Mongabay talks to the founder of Capital Kiwi, a community and Māori-led project that has released more than 250 kiwi into the hills surrounding Wellington. He explains the landscape-scale predator control that made it possible and what it took to get landowners and iwi working together.

items.title: 9/UX puts a classic Macintosh desktop on top of 9front
items.why: Someone looked at Plan 9 and A/UX and decided the obvious thing was to marry them, which is exactly the kind of decision this category exists for. The neat part is that it isn't an emulator: the spatial Finder-ish desktop is built from rio, libdraw, 9P and the plumber, so every app's UI state is just files. Worth a look for the screenshots alone, and more for the design notes.
items.summary: 9/UX is a desktop environment for 9front that borrows the look and conventions of the classic Mac and Apple's A/UX: a global menu bar, spatial windows, consistent dialogs and icons. It is built natively the Plan 9 way, exposing application interfaces through 9P and using namespaces and ndb rather than reimplementing any Apple software.

items.title: Beyond Linux: a sysadmin's tour of the BSDs, illumos and the other free OSes
items.why: A talk given to a Linux Day crowd in Modena that gently points out the rest of the family: FreeBSD, NetBSD, OpenBSD, illumos and friends. The argument is less 'switch' than 'remember why we share code at all', which is very much the late-90s spirit. Good reading for anyone who first met Unix on something that wasn't Linux.
items.summary: Stefano Marinelli, who runs a small open-source consultancy, publishes an adapted version of his Linux Day 2026 talk. He walks through the BSDs, illumos and other alternative operating systems and uses them to reflect on open source as a philosophy and a habit of sharing knowledge, not only a codebase.

items.title: When the churches of Athens argued with each other in print, 1854
items.why: An anonymous 1854 writer gave the churches of Athens voices and let them squabble in a newspaper, which is either the best or worst idea in architectural criticism. Underneath the jokes is a young nation fretting about whether to build like Byzantium or like Bavaria. A lovely odd archive find.
items.summary: Public Domain Review looks at a satirical newspaper piece from 1854 in which the churches of Athens debate one another. Historian Nikos Magouliotis reads the dialogue as a window on Greek anxieties about architectural identity, foreign influence and the new state's relationship to its past.

items.title: Richard Baldwin's 'third unbundling': when offices, not factories, cross borders
items.why: Baldwin's framing is tidy: first goods crossed borders, then factories, and now office work does. Timothy Taylor does his usual thing of walking through one paper without selling a thesis, which makes it a sober way to think about remote work and services trade. No outrage, just a useful mental model.
items.summary: Timothy Taylor summarises a new NBER working paper by Richard Baldwin that describes globalisation as a sequence of three unbundlings. The latest one, enabled by digital tools, lets service and office tasks be done abroad, and the post looks at what that might mean for trade and jobs.

items.title: Bern's Wasserspeier, the rooftop dragon that soaks coin-hunters
items.why: Since 1984 a dragon-like spout on an Old Town roof has been splashing anyone who stoops for the five-franc coins scattered below. It's a prank installation reinstalled every spring, which is very un-Swiss and very charming. One for the list if you're ever wandering the Münstergasse in summer.
items.summary: Atlas Obscura describes the Wasserspeier, an art installation in Bern's Old Town that periodically sprays water into the street from a roof spout shaped like a dragon. Coins left on the pavement tempt passers-by to bend down at just the wrong moment; the artist and homeowner put it up every spring.

items.title: The Last Waltz at fifty, and why it became a Thanksgiving film
items.why: The Band's farewell show was filmed on Thanksgiving Day 1976, and half a century later plenty of people still put it on with the leftovers. No Depression marks the anniversary the day before the holiday, which is good timing. A fine excuse to rewatch the string-band and roots moments between the big-name cameos.
items.summary: No Depression looks back at The Last Waltz, Martin Scorsese's film of The Band's farewell concert at Winterland on Thanksgiving 1976. The piece considers why it remains one of the best-loved music documentaries and how it turned into a holiday viewing tradition.

items.title: In 1904 a musician transcribed MPs' speeches as musical notation
items.why: The Strand sent a musician into the House of Commons to write down speakers' pitch and rhythm on a stave, which is the most Edwardian approach to political commentary imaginable. Some members got a dominant note and a description of their cadence, with not a word about policy. Pure Futility Closet, and a nice reminder that speech has a melody.
items.summary: Futility Closet shares an item from a 1904 issue of The Strand Magazine in which a musician notated the voices of members of Parliament. Each speaker's pitch, pace and inflection was set down in musical notation, with short notes on how each one sounded.

items.title: A new generation of futexes
items.why: The futex is the kernel's most successful bit of minimalism: one integer, one syscall, and every pthread mutex on the planet resting on top. Which is also why changing it takes years of patch series and careful arguing about hash tables and NUMA nodes. Now free to read, and worth it for anyone who has ever stared at a futex_wait in a profile.
items.summary: LWN examines the latest push to rework the kernel's fast userspace mutex interface into a new generation of futex operations. The piece covers what the existing design gets wrong for modern workloads and how the proposed changes try to fix it without breaking the huge amount of code built on futexes.

items.title: Buildroot turns 25
items.why: Buildroot started life as a side tool for testing a tiny C library and quietly became the way a great many embedded boards get their root filesystem. It is the late-90s spirit in its purest form: Makefiles, Kconfig and volunteers, still going a quarter of a century later. Filed under Open source, since it is a project story rather than a kernel one.
items.summary: LWN marks a quarter century of Buildroot, the Makefile-driven system for building complete embedded Linux images from source. The retrospective looks back at how the project grew from its uClibc roots into a widely used build tool with regular releases and long-term support branches.

items.title: Old Java feature phones can still get online, over Bluetooth
items.why: Remember when Bluetooth was going to give us personal area networks and everyone shrugged and bought Wi-Fi instead? Turns out the idea was just waiting for 2G to die. The real trick is Opera Mini's server-side rendering, which does the modern-TLS heavy lifting so a Sony Ericsson does not have to.
items.summary: With 2G networks shutting down, old Java-capable feature phones look stranded, but a hobbyist shows they can still reach the internet through a Bluetooth network served by a Raspberry Pi. Paired with a still-downloadable Java build of Opera Mini, whose rendering happens on a server, a Sony Ericsson handset browses again.

items.title: Curiosity's 49 drill holes, collected in one collage
items.why: Every one of these neat little circles is a sample run through an onboard lab, and together they read like a core log of Gale Crater's climb up Mount Sharp. It is also a quiet tribute to a drill that had a famous mechanical fault years ago and got patched back into service from millions of kilometres away.
items.summary: NASA has assembled images of all 49 holes Curiosity has drilled on Mars as of this month into a single collage. Each hole marks a spot where the rover ground rock into powder for its onboard instruments to analyse during its long traverse.

items.title: Diffractive 'rainbow' solar sails that can steer sideways
items.why: Ordinary solar sails are mirrors, which means sunlight can only shove them more or less straight away from the Sun. A sail patterned to diffract light can turn some of that push sideways, which is the difference between a raft and a sailboat. The Earth-shading angle is speculative, but the optics are lovely.
items.summary: Researchers at the Rochester Institute of Technology have a preprint describing ultra-thin sails that use diffraction, splitting light like a grating, to generate sideways thrust as well as forward push. The technique could make solar sails far more manoeuvrable, and the authors also suggest such films might one day help shade the Earth.

items.title: Birds that are brilliant fliers or swimmers and hopeless on foot
items.why: Evolution rarely gives anyone everything, and birds make the trade-offs unusually visible: legs set far back for diving, or shrunk to near nothing for a life spent on the wing. A good one for a solo birder who has watched a swiftlet colony at dusk and never once seen one stroll.
items.summary: Audubon looks at species such as swifts and loons, which are superbly built for the air or the water but can barely manage on land. The piece explains how body plans tuned for flight or diving leave some birds awkward, or almost helpless, when they have to walk.

items.title: Indianola, the Texas port that received camels and then vanished
items.why: A town that was once Texas's second port, the landing point for the US Army's camel experiment, and is now mostly a historical marker and some beach. The camels are the hook, but the real story is how quickly a booming place can be wiped off the coast. A ghost town you can actually drive to.
items.summary: Indianola on the Texas Gulf coast was once a busy port, where in 1856 the Army landed camels for its short-lived Camel Corps experiment. After Civil War occupation and two devastating hurricanes in 1876 and 1886, the town was abandoned, and today little remains but markers on the shore.

items.title: Kathleen Edwards' Back to Me, twenty years on
items.why: Not one of the favourites, but a Canadian songwriter who writes the kind of precise, bruised songs that sit comfortably next to Caitlin Canty on a playlist. No Depression's criticism fellowship is giving classic roots records the long, careful review they deserve, and this one dwells on how much sadness fits into a well-built chord.
items.summary: A No Depression criticism fellow revisits Kathleen Edwards' 2005 album Back to Me, focusing on its songs of endurance and heartbreak. The review spends time on the quietly devastating Copied Keys and how the record's arrangements carry its emotional weight.

items.title: Martha Wells Book Club reaches The Gate of Gods
items.why: Long before a grumpy security unit made her famous, Wells wrote this fantasy trilogy about a magic-rich kingdom fighting a war it does not understand. Reactor's book club finishes it off this month, and the reviewer's relief at the ending is the best endorsement you could ask for.
items.summary: Reactor's monthly Martha Wells reread arrives at The Gate of Gods, the final book of her Fall of Ile-Rien trilogy. The column sorts through how the many threads resolve for the sorcerers, gods and reluctant heroes, and how well the ending lands.

items.title: Nospeaker makes a MacBook trackpad talk with its haptic motor
items.why: There is no speaker in that trackpad, just a little motor that fakes a click, and someone has driven it fast enough to sing. It is the same spirit as playing tunes on floppy drive steppers: hardware doing a job nobody designed it for. Hacker News liked it, and for once the reason is the hack itself.
items.summary: Nospeaker is a small open-source program that drives the haptic motor under a Force Touch trackpad thousands of times a second, fast enough to produce audible sound. It uses that to speak, sing and act as a playable instrument under your finger.

items.title: BepiColombo arrives at Mercury and settles in for the long orbit
items.why: Getting to the innermost planet is weirdly harder than getting to Jupiter: you spend the whole trip braking against the Sun's pull, which is why this took eight years and a string of flybys. Only MESSENGER has orbited Mercury before, so this is the second proper look at a planet whose oversized iron core still lacks a good explanation. Two orbiters, two agencies, one very hot neighbourhood.
items.summary: The joint European and Japanese BepiColombo mission has reached Mercury after a journey of more than eight years and roughly six billion miles, and controllers are firing its thrusters to enter orbit. It will become only the second spacecraft to circle the planet, mapping its surface and probing its interior to understand its unusually large core.

items.title: A shock wave near the galactic centre may be building stars, and redrawing a spiral arm
items.why: Mapping the galaxy from the inside is like drawing your house's floor plan while locked in the pantry, so revisions are expected. The fun part is that a rotating structure near the centre seems to be shocking gas into forming stars rather than blowing it apart. And part of the Norma arm, a staple of every Milky Way diagram, may be something else entirely.
items.summary: Astronomers report evidence that a large rotating structure near the Milky Way's centre drives shock waves that trigger star formation, where similar regions in other galaxies tend to suppress it. The work also suggests that a stretch of what has been called the Norma spiral arm may instead be a broad star-forming region, which would change how the galaxy's layout is drawn.

items.title: Species spotlight: Wilson's bird-of-paradise in Raja Ampat
items.why: Few birds look as though they were assembled from a paint catalogue quite like this one: a bare turquoise crown, a red back, and two curled tail wires that seem to be on loan from a violin. It lives only on a couple of islands off West Papua, practically next door by Southeast Asian birding standards. The writer's grumbling about rainforests that look like abandoned gardening projects is a bonus.
items.summary: A 10,000 Birds species profile of Wilson's bird-of-paradise, written from a trip to Raja Ampat in West Papua, one of the few places the bird is found. The piece mixes field impressions of the rainforest with a look at this small, startlingly coloured species and its showy courtship.

items.title: Soviet fighter jets parked in a Catalan village garden
items.why: Most villages of sixty people boast a church and some fields. This one also has three Soviet fighters and an American jet in somebody's garden, just off the motorway about an hour from Barcelona. It's the sort of private obsession that turns into a local landmark, and a decent excuse for a road trip.
items.summary: Atlas Obscura describes a small walled village in rural Catalonia where a private collection of retired military aircraft, including three Soviet-built fighters and one American jet, sits on display. The informal museum has become an unlikely attraction for a place with only a few dozen residents.

items.title: XNU Linux runs the macOS kernel as a Linux kernel module
items.why: Someone took Apple's published XNU sources, built the whole kernel as a loadable module, and insmod'ed it into a stock arm64 Linux kernel, where it drives the MMU directly and runs macOS processes alongside Linux ones. No hypervisor, just a small shim lending XNU memory, timers, files and the GPU. It is either brilliant or deranged, and in the best hacker tradition probably both.
items.summary: An experimental project that builds XNU, the open-source core of macOS, and loads it into an unmodified arm64 Linux kernel as a module. A companion module lets XNU borrow Linux's memory, timers, filesystems, networking and GPU, so a full macOS graphical userspace can run natively on the same CPUs as Linux programs.

items.title: Reverse engineering an ALU board from Spacelab's French minicomputer
items.why: Before microprocessors were trusted with anything important, a CPU was a stack of boards full of chips, and Spacelab flew on one of these, a French-built Mitra 125 MS. Ken Shirriff takes a single ALU and register card and works out what every part does, which is about as close as you can get to holding 1980s spaceflight computing in your hand. Skip the primers; the board photos are the point.
items.summary: Ken Shirriff examines one of the processor boards from the Mitra 125 MS, the minicomputer that controlled Spacelab, the reusable laboratory carried in the Space Shuttle's payload bay. Its 16-bit processor was built from several boards of discrete logic chips, and he traces how this one implements part of the arithmetic logic unit.

items.title: The Morning Paper on DREAM: consistency guarantees for distributed reactive programs
items.why: Reactive programming is lovely until the dependency graph spans machines, at which point every update becomes a little consistency problem in disguise. This 2014 paper, revisited in Adrian Colyer's archive, lays out a ladder of guarantees, from anything-goes through glitch-freedom to atomic, and measures what each rung costs. Anyone who has argued about causal versus total ordering will recognise the trade-offs…
items.summary: A Morning Paper write-up of DREAM, a middleware for distributed reactive programming that lets developers choose among several consistency models for how changes propagate between dependent values on different nodes. The paper compares the guarantees and the network and latency overhead each one brings.

items.title: Bunnicula at forty-odd: the vampire rabbit that drains vegetables
items.why: A rabbit with fangs that sucks the juice out of tomatoes is a perfect children's-book premise, and it came from two people who simply loved vampire movies. Judith Tarr's SFF Bestiary column, written by someone who also keeps animals, takes it seriously as a piece of genre storytelling. Pleasant nostalgia with a pale white tomato on the side.
items.summary: Judith Tarr revisits Bunnicula, the 1979 children's novel by Deborah and James Howe about a family pet rabbit suspected of being a vampire. She looks at how the couple's fondness for horror films sparked the idea and at what makes the book work.

items.title: Physicists send a message through a wall using a lift counterweight and gravity
items.why: The bandwidth is terrible and the hardware is a building's elevator, which is exactly what makes this delightful. Shuttling a 1.8-tonne counterweight between two floors to encode ones and zeros, picked up by a gravimeter in the bathroom next door, is about the most physical covert channel imaginable. Nothing short of moving the Earth can jam it.
items.summary: Researchers at the University of Queensland transmitted a binary message through a brick wall by moving an elevator, and its heavy counterweight, between two floors. A sensitive gravimeter in a neighbouring room detected the tiny changes in the local gravitational field and decoded the bits.

items.title: A pair of mislabelled bones in a Brazilian collection turn out to be a new silesaurid
items.why: Silesaurids sit right at the root of the dinosaur family tree, close enough that palaeontologists still argue over which side of the line they fall on, so every new one matters more than its size suggests. Also notable: this one was found not in the field but in a museum drawer, filed as indeterminate and keeping company with cynodont scraps.
items.summary: Two bones long catalogued as unidentifiable in a Brazilian fossil collection have been described as a new silesaurid species, Itaguyra occulta. The find helps fill a gap in the early record of the lineage closely related to the first dinosaurs.

items.title: Europa's sodium cloud seems to come from its buried ocean
items.why: Europa trails a thin haze of sodium around Jupiter, and where it comes from bears on the big question of what the hidden ocean is made of. If the salt really is welling up from below, every spectrum of that cloud becomes a free, long-distance sample of the water nobody can drill into yet.
items.summary: Astronomers using a spectrometer at the Keck Observatory have new evidence that the sodium escaping Europa originates in the moon's subsurface ocean rather than from outside sources. It offers an indirect way to study the ocean's chemistry from Earth.

items.title: LISA could spot exoplanets by the wobble they leave in gravitational waves
items.why: Transits, wobbles and microlensing are the usual ways to find planets; this proposes listening for them instead. A planet tugging on a pair of compact stars as they spiral together would leave a faint modulation in the signal, which is a lovely example of an instrument built for one thing quietly turning out to be good at another.
items.summary: New research suggests that ESA's planned space-based gravitational wave observatory, LISA, could detect planets orbiting merging compact binaries. The planet's small pull on the binary would leave a measurable signature in the gravitational waves it emits.

items.title: China's mangroves have more than doubled, and bird species have followed
items.why: A rare piece of conservation news with numbers going the right way: recorded bird species in China's mangroves rose from under 150 to nearly 400 as the forests came back. Part of the recovery came from turning old aquaculture ponds back into mangrove, a trick worth watching for the coasts of Penang too.
items.summary: Mangrove cover in China more than doubled between 1998 and 2020 after decades of heavy losses, according to a new study, and the number of bird species recorded in those areas more than doubled with it. Reserves, restoration of former fish ponds and a warmer, wetter climate all helped.

items.title: A Wi-Fi adapter for the Super Nintendo that plugs into the controller port
items.why: Nintendo never really put the SNES online outside Japan's satellite experiment, so naturally someone has done it through the joypad sockets. Thirty kilobytes a second over a controller port is roughly the bandwidth of a decent 1990s modem, which feels about right for the machine.
items.summary: A hobbyist has built a wireless network adapter for the SNES that talks to the console through its front controller ports. It pairs an RP2350 microcontroller for the console link with an ESP32-C3 for Wi-Fi, giving a data link of around 30 kB/s.

items.title: Ladybird, the browser with a from-scratch engine, reaches alpha
items.why: A brand-new browser engine, not a Chromium or WebKit descendant, written by a small community that started out building a hobby OS, now downloadable for macOS and Linux. It is exactly the kind of gloriously unreasonable project the late-90s web was built on, and the team openly asks people to break it.
items.summary: The Ladybird project has released its first alpha, a browser built on its own engine written from the ground up. Some sites won't work and crashes are expected, and users can report broken pages and crash reports from within the browser.

items.title: The Summit House, a 19th-century mountaintop hotel above the Connecticut River
items.why: Before national parks, New Englanders took their sublime scenery from hotel porches, and this one on Mount Holyoke drew Jenny Lind, Alexander Graham Bell and assorted Transcendentalists. It sits in the Pioneer Valley, an easy add to any Concord and Walden pilgrimage, and the view over the river oxbow is the one Thomas Cole made famous.
items.summary: The Summit House, also called the Prospect House, opened in 1851 on Mount Holyoke in what is now Skinner State Park in Hadley, Massachusetts. Once a fashionable retreat reached by a mountain railway, it now anchors a park with trails and wide views over the valley.

items.title: Why Plymouth Rock is smaller than its reputation
items.why: Just in time for Thanksgiving, a look at New England's most famous disappointment. The rock's story is better than the rock: none of the Pilgrims' own accounts mention it, it was only singled out more than a century later, and it has since been split, hauled around town and chipped away by souvenir hunters.
items.summary: Boston.com looks at why Plymouth Rock, the boulder said to mark where the Pilgrims came ashore, leaves so many visitors underwhelmed. The answer lies in its history: a modest stone with a large legend, shrunk further over the centuries.

items.title: Soddy's hexlet: the necklace of spheres that always closes at six
items.why: Pack spheres around two touching neighbours inside a bigger one and the chain always loops back after exactly six, no matter their sizes. Bonus points to Frederick Soddy, a Nobel chemist who announced the result in Nature in verse, and to the Japanese temple-geometry tablets that had it more than a century earlier.
items.summary: A short piece on the hexlet, a ring of six spheres each tangent to its neighbours, to two inner spheres and to an enclosing sphere. Soddy published it in 1937, though Japanese mathematicians knew it by at least 1822.

items.title: The Art of Knitting, an 1892 manual of stitches and lore, now free online
items.why: The Smithsonian and the Internet Archive have digitised a Victorian knitting manual, and old pattern books are their own kind of code listing: terse, abbreviated, and assuming the reader already knows the runtime. Worth a browse even if you have never held a needle.
items.summary: Kottke points to a digitised copy of The Art of Knitting from 1892, made available by the Smithsonian and the Internet Archive. The book collects patterns, stitches and knitting lore from more than 130 years ago.

items.title: Black holes may be born from stars that simply collapse, no supernova required
items.why: Astronomers have long expected big stars to go out with a bang, so a statistical hole in the merger catalogue is a nice bit of detective work. The interesting part is the method: nobody watched a star vanish, they inferred it from the masses of black holes caught colliding.
items.summary: A pattern in the masses of 257 black hole mergers detected by gravitational waves points to a population of black holes that formed when massive stars collapsed quietly instead of exploding. If it holds, these failed supernovae could account for a large share of the black holes out there.

items.title: Astronomers catch a luminous red nova as it happens, for the first time
items.why: Common-envelope binaries are one of those stages of stellar life that shows up in every textbook diagram and almost never in a telescope. Catching one in the act gives the theorists something real to fit their drag-and-spiral models against.
items.summary: When one star in a close pair swells and wraps its companion in a shared envelope of gas, the drag can pull the two together until they merge in an outburst called a luminous red nova. Astronomers have now observed one of these events unfold in real time rather than reconstructing it afterwards.

items.title: A birder's field guide to the 60 bird species of GTA 6
items.why: Audubon sending a writer into Vice City with binoculars is the most wholesome use of a crime game imaginable. The fun is in how seriously it's taken: species counts, habitats and how faithfully the developers rendered Florida's real birdlife.
items.summary: An Audubon writer spent launch night tracking down every one of the roughly 60 bird species in the new Grand Theft Auto, a game set in a fictional take on Miami and the Florida coast. The guide covers what turns up where and how closely the digital birds match the real thing.

items.title: Smooth-coated otters are turning up along Kuala Lumpur's Klang River
items.why: Close to home and a rare piece of good urban-wildlife news: otters playing on a sandbar under a KL highway. Nobody is quite sure why they've come back, which makes the story more interesting than a tidy cleanup victory lap.
items.summary: Small family groups of smooth-coated otters, a species listed as vulnerable, are now seen regularly in parts of Kuala Lumpur, including stretches of the once badly polluted Klang River. Their return has raised hopes about the river's recovery, though explanations for why they've appeared vary.

items.title: The Brothers Brick reviews LEGO Star Wars 75480 Duel on Bespin
items.why: The companion to the Mustafar set, and arguably the better scene: the gantry, the reactor shaft and that line of dialogue. Worth reading for how the designers squeeze a vertigo-inducing set into a modest box, and for the backstory of the earlier region-locked convention version.
items.summary: A review of the Cloud City duel set from LEGO's 50th-anniversary Star Wars wave, released alongside the Mustafar duel. The Brothers Brick weighs the build and minifigures against an earlier exclusive version of the same scene that ended up region-locked during the pandemic.

items.title: Network theorists pin down when local failover rules can guarantee delivery
items.why: Fast reroute is the sort of thing every router does and few people think hard about, so it's satisfying to see the theory get a clean answer. Quanta frames it with the Arpanet's two-character crash in 1969, which is a fitting place to start a story about networks that refuse to fall over.
items.summary: Researchers have worked out which network shapes allow perfect resilience: forwarding rules set in advance, using only what a router can see locally, that still deliver every packet as long as some path between source and destination survives. Quanta walks through the problem and what the result means for real networks.

items.title: Hiding an IRC server on TCP port zero
items.why: A proper Hackaday rabbit hole: the port number everyone treats as reserved turns out to be perfectly usable if you go around the socket API. Anyone who has read the bind path in the kernel will enjoy seeing it sidestepped with a firewall rule.
items.summary: Port zero is almost never used, and asking the Linux kernel to bind it just hands you a random ephemeral port instead. One tinkerer got around that with nftables port mapping, putting a plain-text IRC server on port zero, and found that only about a quarter of a percent of hosts on the internet answer there at all.

items.title: Jeff Geerling joins the NTP Pool with a GNSS-disciplined home time server
items.why: Volunteer infrastructure in the old spirit: one person with a Raspberry Pi, a rooftop antenna and a timing-grade receiver deciding to share good time with the world. Note the sensible layering, a Stratum 2 public server fed from the Stratum 1 box rather than exposing the precious one directly.
items.summary: Geerling built a Stratum 1 time server from a Raspberry Pi, a TimeHAT board and a u-blox timing GNSS module wired to an outdoor antenna, then joined the volunteer NTP Pool with a public Stratum 2 server that syncs from it. He walks through the setup and encourages others to contribute their own servers.

items.title: Spelunkr turns the Internet Archive's forgotten videos into a TV network
items.why: The Internet Archive holds a staggering amount of video that nobody ever stumbles across, and a channel-flipping interface is a clever way to make browsing feel like idle late-night TV. A good antidote to the infinite scroll, which is rather the point of this feed.
items.summary: Spelunkr is a free web project that strings obscure videos from the Internet Archive's collections into continuous channels you can flip between, like broadcast television. It drew a warm reception on Hacker News.

items.title: The floor of one of medieval Nubia's largest cathedrals emerges in Old Dongola
items.why: Christian Nubia is one of the great underrated chapters of medieval history, and Old Dongola was the capital of the kingdom of Makuria. That archaeologists can keep working there at all right now is a small marvel in itself.
items.summary: Archaeologists working at Old Dongola in northern Sudan have exposed the original floor of a huge medieval cathedral, among the biggest churches of its era anywhere. The building belonged to Makuria, a Christian Nubian kingdom that flourished along the Nile for centuries.

items.title: A skull dug up near a South African village in 2018 turns out to be a new early sauropodomorph
items.why: Dinosaur news, and the good kind: a nearly complete skull, which in early sauropodomorphs is rarer than a quiet Lobsters thread. The fossil sat in collections for years before anyone gave it a proper look, a reminder that half of palaeontology happens in museum drawers rather than in the field.
items.summary: A nearly complete skull found in 2018 near a village in South Africa has been described as a new species of early sauropodomorph, named Nyana rooiwalensis, from the lineage that later gave rise to the giant long-necked sauropods. Skulls from these early forms are uncommon, so the find adds useful detail to how the group's heads and feeding evolved.

items.title: Folk Alley's FreshCuts hour for 13 November, with Brittany Haas on the playlist
items.why: Brittany Haas turns up on this week's FreshCuts list, which is reason enough to hit play. The rest of the hour leans toward the acoustic and the banjo-forward, including a bluegrass instrumental credited to Alison Brown, so it is a sound bet for an idle afternoon.
items.summary: Folk Alley's weekly FreshCuts radio hour, hosted by Cindy Howes, rounds up new folk, bluegrass and Americana releases. The 13 November edition includes a new song from Antje Duvekot, a James Felice track, a banjo tune from Kristin Scott Benson, Gena Britt and Alison Brown, and Brittany Haas among the featured artists.

items.title: Voyager 1 is now a full light-day from Earth
items.why: Nearly half a century after launch, Voyager 1 has crossed a tidy milestone: a command sent from Earth now takes about a day to arrive, and the reply takes another day to come back. Anyone who has debugged over a slow serial link will feel for the flight software team, who still keep a 1970s machine running on a shrinking power budget.
items.summary: Voyager 1 has travelled roughly 16 billion miles, far enough that radio signals moving at light speed need around 24 hours to cover the distance. The probe, launched in 1977, is in interstellar space and still sending data, though its power supply keeps dwindling and engineers continue to switch off systems to keep it going.

items.title: What if Netscape had bolted SSL onto HTTP instead of slipping it underneath
items.why: A pleasant bit of protocol alternate history: what the web might look like if encryption had been negotiated inside HTTP rather than as a separate layer below it. The author makes a good case that SNI is just a Host header that had to be reinvented, and owns up cheerfully to the anachronisms needed to make the parallel universe work.
items.summary: An essay imagines a 1995 in which Netscape waited for HTTP to grow an upgrade mechanism and a Host header, and then secured web traffic from within HTTP on the usual port. It walks through how the handshake would have looked and which later fixes to TLS might never have been needed.

items.title: Gliver, a hackable Guile Scheme window manager for Wayland, rounds out a Guix desktop
items.why: This is the late-90s spirit in a nutshell: a tiling window manager you can poke at from a live REPL while it runs, written so that people are invited to read the code rather than fear it. It is version 0.0.something and the author is upfront about bugs, which only adds to the charm.
items.summary: Christine Lemmer-Webber writes about Gliver, a Wayland window manager in the style of StumpWM and Emacs, written in Guile Scheme and still in early releases. It is live-hackable through a socket REPL, has built-in help for finding keys and commands, and is on its way into Guix as the missing piece of a fully Scheme-flavoured desktop.

items.title: Melting years of coffee capsules into a cast aluminium moka pot
items.why: There is a certain poetry in turning single-use pods back into the stovetop pot they replaced. It worked, sort of: the pot brews, but the cast metal leaks like a sieve, and the whole thing retired with honour as a flower pot. Proper maker energy, failure included.
items.summary: A maker collected a few years' worth of aluminium coffee capsules, melted them down in a small furnace to make ingots, and cast the two halves of a moka pot using 3D-printed lost-PLA moulds. With a store-bought filter and seal it does make coffee, but the casting is porous enough that much of the water escapes, so the pot ended up holding plants instead.

items.title: All Change Please: Adrian Colyer on what fast networks and persistent memory do to distributed systems design
items.why: A 2016 Morning Paper piece that reads well with hindsight: RDMA, non-volatile memory and fast storage were arriving together, and the numbers from systems like FaRM, DrTM and RAMCloud suggested old assumptions about where the bottleneck lives were about to go stale. Worth checking which predictions aged well and which are still waiting.
items.summary: Adrian Colyer surveys how changes in networking, memory, storage and processors were set to reshape the design of data-centre systems, drawing on results from several research systems built on RDMA and in-memory storage. He argues that transaction throughput and latency figures once thought impossible were becoming routine, forcing a rethink of distributed systems design.

items.title: Covers from Amauta, the Lima magazine that tried to give Peru its own modern look
items.why: Bold, graphic covers from a short-lived 1920s magazine that mixed Andean imagery with modernist design. Even if you skip the politics, the art stands up on its own, and the Public Domain Review gallery is a lovely place to linger.
items.summary: The Public Domain Review gathers cover designs from Amauta, the magazine founded by José Carlos Mariátegui and published in Lima between 1926 and 1930. The covers blend Indigenous Peruvian motifs with avant-garde graphic styles, reflecting the magazine's aim of building a distinctly Peruvian modern culture.

items.title: 10,000 Birds profiles Armonía, Bolivia's bird conservation group
items.why: A calm, practical read on the people doing the unglamorous work of keeping birds around. Bolivia is one of the richest bird countries on the planet and gets far less attention than its neighbours, so this is a good window into how a small national organisation has kept at it for three decades.
items.summary: The blog's new series on global bird conservation organisations opens with a Q and A with Armonía, a Bolivian nonprofit founded in 1996. The group describes its main conservation work, which includes efforts for threatened species and the habitats they depend on.

items.title: The 2026 Xingyun Awards for Chinese science fiction announced in Chengdu
items.why: Chengdu has quietly become one of the capitals of the genre, and the Xingyun Awards are a good map of what Chinese readers are excited about. Handy for anyone who finished Liu Cixin and wondered where to go next.
items.summary: The World Chinese Science Fiction Association announced the winners of the 17th Xingyun Awards at a ceremony in Chengdu on 15 November. Prizes cover the best novel, novella, short story, translated work and non-fiction, among other categories.

items.title: Light sails meet an unexpected headwind at three-quarters of light speed
items.why: Interstellar light-sail mission concepts usually treat the laser as pure push. This work finds that once a sail is moving fast enough, some of the scattered light starts acting as drag, which is the sort of relativistic fine print every Breakthrough Starshot spreadsheet will now need a row for. Clarke would have enjoyed the plot twist.
items.summary: Researchers modelling laser-driven solar sails report that at around 75 percent of light speed, part of the light scattered by the sail begins to slow it rather than speed it up. The effect could complicate plans to send gram-scale probes to nearby stars, and sail designs may need to account for it.

items.title: ESA's Hera starts mapping the asteroid that DART hit
items.why: DART was the punch; Hera is the forensic team showing up afterwards with a measuring tape. The spacecraft is flying careful rectangular passes around Didymos and Dimorphos to work out whether the 2022 impact left a crater or rearranged the whole rubble pile. Planetary defence, done the patient way.
items.summary: Europe's Hera probe has arrived at the binary asteroid system where NASA's DART spacecraft crashed into the moonlet Dimorphos in 2022. Its close-up survey aims to measure what the impact actually did to the small body, which matters for knowing how well the deflection technique would work on a threatening asteroid.

items.title: Three photos of the Western Parotia, a bird of paradise from the Arfak Mountains
items.why: Parotias are the birds of paradise that dance: the males clear a stage on the forest floor, flare a skirt of feathers and wag head plumes tipped like little paddles. These shots come from the Arfak Mountains of West Papua, close enough to the Malay archipelago to count as a neighbour. A quiet three-photo post, which is exactly the right dose.
items.summary: 10,000 Birds shares a short set of photographs of the Western Parotia, taken in the Arfak Mountains of West Papua in Indonesian New Guinea. The species is one of the birds of paradise, known for the males' elaborate courtship displays.

items.title: bitluni builds a twenty-cent USB graphics adapter around one microcontroller
items.why: This is the good kind of absurd: a USB-to-composite-video adapter whose only active part is a cheap CH570 microcontroller, with both the USB-C plug and the RCA connector made out of the circuit board itself. Calling it a GPU is cheeky, and also technically defensible. Demoscene energy, hardware edition.
items.summary: Maker bitluni designed a tiny PCB that takes video over USB and outputs analogue composite video, using a single low-cost microcontroller plus a few passive components. The connectors are formed from the board's own copper and edge shape, keeping the parts cost to pennies.

items.title: Bringing up NixOS on a cheap RISC-V board bought off Alibaba
items.why: Someone went looking for an FPGA devkit, ended up with an eight-core RISC-V board instead, and turned it into a NixOS build server. Board bring-up notes like this are a good snapshot of where RISC-V distro support really stands once you leave QEMU behind. Expect device trees, patience and small victories.
items.summary: A blogger documents getting NixOS running on a Zhihe Computing A210 RISC-V board picked up from Alibaba, with the aim of using it as a native build machine. The write-up covers what works, what needed coaxing, and the state of RISC-V support in NixOS on real hardware.

items.title: Marc Brooker on how Dynamo, DynamoDB and Aurora DSQL actually relate
items.why: Three systems, two of them sharing a name and none of them sharing an architecture. Brooker, who was there for much of it, lays the 2007 SOSP Dynamo paper next to DynamoDB and DSQL and compares how each gets its availability, consistency and scaling. Worth it for anyone who has had to explain to a colleague that DynamoDB is not the Dynamo paper.
items.summary: A post comparing the design of Amazon's original Dynamo key-value store, the DynamoDB managed service, and the newer Aurora DSQL distributed SQL database. It walks through how each system achieves its key properties and points to the papers describing them.

items.title: How did Robinson Crusoe find only one footprint?
items.why: One of literature's most famous plot devices is also one of its least explicable: a single footprint on a beach, with no others leading to or from it. Futility Closet picks up John Sutherland's puzzle over how Defoe's scene could physically happen. Bonus points for whichever theory you find least ridiculous.
items.summary: A short Futility Closet post on the lone footprint Crusoe discovers in Defoe's novel, and the puzzle of how one print could appear without any trail. It draws on John Sutherland's book of literary puzzles, which floats some colourful explanations.

items.title: No Depression on Neal Casal's Book of Stories
items.why: Casal spent most of his career making other people's bands sound better, from the Cardinals to the Chris Robinson Brotherhood. This review argues his own songwriting deserves the same attention, and makes the case calmly rather than with hype. A good prompt to dig into a solo catalogue that a lot of roots fans skipped.
items.summary: No Depression reviews Book of Stories, a release of Neal Casal's songs, and uses it to look back at his underappreciated solo work. The reviewer contrasts his reputation as a trusted guitarist in other people's groups with the craft of his own records.

items.title: Guaita, the oldest of San Marino's Three Towers
items.why: A thousand-year-old fortress perched on Monte Titano, double-walled, with a chapel to the patron saint of artillerymen and a stint as a prison until 1970. It also sits on the national flag, which is a fair indication of how much it matters locally. One of the more photogenic reasons to detour into a microstate.
items.summary: Wikipedia's picture of the day shows Guaita, the oldest and best known of the Three Towers of San Marino on Monte Titano. Built in the 11th century and rebuilt several times, it served as a refuge during sieges and partly as a prison, and is now part of a World Heritage Site.

items.title: Walter Crane's cartoons for the 1896 International Workers' Congress
items.why: Walter Crane is best known for picture books and Arts and Crafts design, but he also drew allegorical cartoons for the labour movement, all banners, angels and flowing robes. The Public Domain Review has a set made as keepsakes for a London congress. Read it as design history: the same line that decorated nurseries, aimed at a very different audience.
items.summary: The Public Domain Review presents illustrations Walter Crane produced in 1896 as souvenirs for delegates to the International Workers' Congress. The images use his characteristic allegorical style to celebrate labour, and show a lesser-known side of the illustrator's work.

items.title: The Simons Observatory opens its eyes on the cosmic microwave background
items.why: Every few years a new telescope on a high, dry plateau promises to find the faint swirl that inflation should have left in the oldest light, and every few years the dust in our own galaxy gets the last laugh. This one has the sensitivity to settle it either way, which is the interesting part: a null result would be news too.
items.summary: The Simons Observatory, an array of telescopes in Chile's Atacama Desert, has started surveying the cosmic microwave background. Its main quarry is a particular polarisation pattern that primordial gravitational waves would leave behind, which would be strong evidence for cosmic inflation.

items.title: Researchers 3D-print simulated Moon dust into interlocking building bricks
items.why: Hauling bricks to the Moon costs roughly their weight in gold, so the plan has always been to make them there out of the grey stuff that gets into everything. The bricks clip together like the plastic kind, though the researchers are candid that they still crumble too easily to bet a habitat on.
items.summary: A research team has 3D-printed lunar regolith into interlocking blocks that fit together like toy bricks, as a possible way to build bases from material already on the Moon. The blocks are experimental and need to be made stronger before they could carry real loads.

items.title: Heather Littlefield's Wildflowers, a road-worn country record that sneaks up on you
items.why: No Depression makes the case for the kind of album that doesn't announce itself, written by someone who has spent a decade playing bars rather than chasing a moment. Worth a listen on a slow evening, which is roughly what it was built for.
items.summary: A review of Wildflowers, the new album from country songwriter Heather Littlefield. The reviewer hears songs shaped by more than ten years of touring small venues, with an unhurried, lived-in confidence.

items.title: Fencing off Go: static checks for deadlock and safety in channel programs, via The Morning Paper
items.why: Adrian Colyer takes a POPL paper full of behavioural types and makes it readable for people who just want to know whether their goroutines will wedge. The trick is a fencing restriction that keeps the model finite enough to check, and the question worth chewing on is how much real Go code fits inside the fence.
items.summary: A 2017 Morning Paper summary of Lange and colleagues' work on verifying Go programs that communicate over channels. Their tool extracts a behavioural model from the code and checks it for liveness and channel safety, given a restriction that keeps the state space bounded.

items.title: Custom firmware gives a Rohde and Schwarz CMU200 analyser a second life on the ham bench
items.why: Lab-grade RF gear tends to retire to the surplus market with its abilities frozen at whatever the vendor shipped. Here one ham decided that was a software problem and added a tracking generator, broadcast FM with RDS decoding, and a set of amateur radio test routines.
items.summary: A radio amateur has written custom firmware for the CMU200 and CMU300 communications analysers. It adds a tracking generator, wideband FM reception with RDS decoding, ham radio test tools modelled on ARRL guidelines, and networking features.

items.title: Edward Weston's Nautilus, a single shell that helped define modernist photography
items.why: Today's Wikipedia picture is one of the most famous still lifes ever made: a shell, a dark background, and a very long exposure. Notice how it reads as almost anatomical, and remember that one of its 28 prints first changed hands for ten dollars.
items.summary: A 1927 black-and-white photograph by Edward Weston of a nautilus shell standing on end, inspired by Henrietta Shore's shell paintings. Weston used long exposures and careful framing to bring out the shell's form, and the image marked a turning point in his modernist work.

items.title: Six LinkedIn posts, as written by birds
items.why: 10,000 Birds imagines our feathered friends discovering the professional networking voice, all long-term vision and embracing change. It's short, silly and a fine palate cleanser; anyone who has watched a heron wait an hour for one fish will agree they really do think in decades.
items.summary: A short humour piece from 10,000 Birds presenting mock LinkedIn posts in the voices of various birds, each one a parody of corporate self-improvement prose.

items.title: Esi Edugyan on the history of Alberta and how it finds its way into fiction
items.why: Edugyan, two-time Giller winner, talks about the less expected sides of Alberta's past and what a novelist does with them. It's the kind of place-is-the-point piece this category exists for, and at under fifteen minutes it fits nicely between other things.
items.summary: An episode of the Atlas Obscura Podcast in which Canadian novelist Esi Edugyan explores Alberta's history and the ways it has shaped fiction. The show runs under fifteen minutes.

items.title: Futility Closet's matchstick puzzle: move one stick to fix the equation
items.why: A proper idle-moment pick: one picture, one rule, and an answer hidden behind a click. Resist the urge to peek for at least two minutes; the obvious moves are all wrong, which is half the fun.
items.summary: A classic matchstick puzzle showing an incorrect equation built from sticks. The challenge is to move exactly one matchstick so the equation becomes true, with the solution available on the page.

items.title: Brookline police issue guidance on what to do when an owl comes at you
items.why: Brookline has spent years learning to coexist with aggressive wild turkeys, and now an owl has apparently joined the neighbourhood's roster of feathered enforcers. Universal Hub notes the police advice sounds a lot like the turkey advice, which is either reassuring or a sign the birds are coordinating.
items.summary: Brookline police have put out advice for residents on handling an owl swooping at them. Universal Hub points out the guidance closely resembles what the town already tells people about confrontational turkeys.

items.title: Nashville Scene names a Punch Brothers show a critic's pick
items.why: Favourite-band rule, and the autumn tour has reached the city where half the string-band world lives anyway. A critic's pick in Nashville is a slightly tougher endorsement to earn than most, given the local competition. Another dot on the map before the PB&J dates with Jeff Tweedy.
items.summary: The Nashville Scene has flagged an upcoming Punch Brothers concert as one of its critic's picks. The listing is brief, a recommendation for the band's stop in town on its current tour rather than a full review.

items.title: Simulations offer an explanation for the lopsided magnetic fields of Uranus and Neptune
items.why: Voyager 2 flew past both ice giants in the 1980s and handed back magnetic fields that were tilted and off-centre in ways no tidy dynamo theory liked. Forty years on, the models finally have something to say. The fun detail is that those poles might wander by tens of degrees within a human lifetime, which makes Earth's slow reversals look positively sedate.
items.summary: New computer simulations of the extreme pressures and temperatures deep inside Uranus and Neptune suggest the material there conducts electricity in unusual ways. That could produce the strongly tilted, off-centre magnetic fields Voyager 2 measured, and implies the magnetic poles may shift surprisingly quickly.

items.title: Autumn birding in Holland, as the passage migrants leave and the winter crowd moves in
items.why: A gentle seasonal dispatch from the 10,000 Birds crew in the Netherlands, written with the honesty of someone who admits that sometimes he just doesn't know. That shoulder season between migration and winter is when a single cold snap reshuffles everything. Good reading for a solo birder on the other side of the world, if only to compare notes on waders.
items.summary: A birder in the Netherlands looks back on late autumn, after the peak of migration has passed and wintering birds are arriving. The post wanders through plovers, gulls, waders and falcons and how weather can change what turns up from one day to the next.

items.title: The Brothers Brick reviews LEGO's new Rebel Y-Wing Starfighter
items.why: The Y-Wing is the scrappy workhorse of the Rebel fleet, and LEGO hasn't given it a standalone set since the well-loved 2017 version. The review weighs whether the new one, part of the run of Star Wars anniversary sets, was worth the wait. Spoiler buried in the headline: the reviewer thinks the design earns its gold star.
items.summary: A hands-on review of LEGO Star Wars set 75478, a new Rebel Y-Wing Starfighter due out on January 1. The reviewer compares it with the 2017 Y-Wing that preceded it and judges how the new build, part of the franchise's 50th-anniversary range, holds up.

items.title: Squeezing Postgres into a single binary, so it can live like SQLite
items.why: Everyone who self-hosts things knows the small sinking feeling when the README says step one is to stand up a Postgres server. This is a hobbyist's attempt to make the big database behave like the embeddable one: point it at a directory and go. The interesting part is less the result than the plumbing it takes to make a client-server system pretend otherwise.
items.summary: The author describes packaging PostgreSQL into a single self-contained executable, so that local and self-hosted software can use it the way SQLite is used, without running and administering a separate server. The post walks through the motivation and the approach.

items.title: An ESP32 brings an old amber MDA monitor back as a wireless terminal
items.why: There is no practical reason to drive a monochrome display adapter monitor in this decade, and that is precisely the point. Most of the work turned out to be software, plus one bodge wire and an afternoon with an oscilloscope chasing timings. The retro command-line interface on top is the cherry.
items.summary: Hackaday covers a hobbyist who connected a vintage MDA monochrome monitor to an ESP32 board, turning it into a wireless terminal. Getting the board's output to match the old monitor's signal took one hardware tweak and careful timing work, and he has shared the result as a fork of an existing terminal project.

items.title: Luke Howard's essay on clouds, the work that gave us cumulus, stratus and cirrus
items.why: A Quaker pharmacist with a weather habit sat down and gave the sky a Latin vocabulary that we still use every day. Goethe was so taken with it that he wrote poems about Howard. The Public Domain Review has the illustrated plates, which are lovely in that early-science, slightly hopeful way.
items.summary: The Public Domain Review presents an edition of Luke Howard's essay on the classification of clouds, the first systematic cloud taxonomy, along with its illustrations. The collection notes Goethe's admiration for Howard and the poem he wrote in his honour.

items.title: A Trail Gone Cold: Iceland, an island of long genealogies and few newcomers
items.why: Damn Interesting does what it does best here: a long, unhurried read about a corner of history most people never think about. Iceland's late settlement and tiny trickle of later arrivals make it a peculiar laboratory for the past. Settle in with a coffee; these pieces reward it.
items.summary: A long-form Damn Interesting article that starts from Iceland's unusual history: settled only in the 9th century, remote, and with very little migration since. From there it follows a historical and scientific puzzle rooted in that isolated population.

items.title: Philcon hands out the 2026 Frank R. Paul Awards for science fiction art
items.why: Frank R. Paul painted the covers that taught early readers what the future looked like, all ray guns and impossible cities. An award in his name is a nice way to keep the pulp-art lineage visible. The trophy itself is a 3D print of one of his own robots wrecking a car, which is exactly the right amount of whimsy.
items.summary: File 770 reports the winners of this year's Frank R. Paul Awards, presented at Philcon on November 20 to honour science fiction and fantasy art. Each winner receives a trophy modelled on a robot from a 1935 Wonder Stories cover by Paul.

items.title: The National Underground Railroad Freedom Center, on the Ohio River in Cincinnati
items.why: Not a quirky stop, but a worthwhile one. Cincinnati sat right on the line where the Ohio River separated slave states from free ones, so the museum stands near where many people actually made the crossing. It calls itself a museum of conscience, and it tells the story through the people who ran the escape routes as much as through those who fled.
items.summary: Atlas Obscura describes the National Underground Railroad Freedom Center in Cincinnati, a museum on the banks of the Ohio River devoted to the history of slavery in the United States and the Underground Railroad. The city was a major crossing point for people escaping north.

items.title: Lean and Mathlib maintainers certify a machine-checked proof of the Riemann Hypothesis
items.why: A week ago this would have been the setup for a joke. Instead the Lean community has put its name to a statement that a 17-million-line formal proof of the Riemann Hypothesis checks out, statement and all, and the mathematical web is having the best kind of weekend. Worth noticing how much of the statement is about process: what exactly was verified, against which criteria, and by whom.
items.summary: Levent Alpöge released a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis as a Lean library on November 20, depending only on Mathlib. Members of the Lean and Mathlib communities spent the following day checking it and have issued a joint statement certifying that both the formal statement of the conjecture and its proof are correct.

items.title: Webb catches the aftermath of one star swallowing another in Andromeda
items.why: Stellar mergers are usually something you infer after the fact from a strange leftover. Here astronomers caught one in a neighbouring galaxy and had Webb looking within seven weeks, which in this business counts as rushing to the scene. The infrared view of the debris is where the new detail lives.
items.summary: In the Andromeda galaxy, a small star spiralled into a giant companion some 18,000 times brighter than the Sun, setting off a violent eruption. The James Webb Space Telescope observed the scene 47 days later, giving astronomers a close look at how two stars combine into one.

items.title: The rise and fall of IBM's System/4 Pi, the computers that flew the Space Shuttle
items.why: Flight software has to run on something, and for the Shuttle that something was a family of IBM aerospace machines with a wonderfully grandiose name. Ken Shirriff traces the line from its origins to the AP-101B units in the avionics bay, with the usual photos of real hardware. Read it for the redundancy story: four computers voting, and a fifth waiting in case they all agreed on the wrong thing.
items.summary: An illustrated history of IBM's System/4 Pi family of aerospace computers, built around the AP-101B models that controlled the Space Shuttle from its first launch in 1981. The piece covers how the family came about, where else it flew, and why it eventually faded out.

items.title: Lundy, the Bristol Channel island where seabirds came back and fishermen helped draw the lines
items.why: Conservation stories tend to come in two flavours, fences or failure, so a third one is welcome. Lundy got its seabirds back over decades while keeping a working fishing community, and the fishermen were in the room when the UK's first no-take zone was drawn. A short video piece, calm and hopeful.
items.summary: Mongabay's video team visits Lundy, a rugged island between Wales and England, where decades of conservation work have brought back thousands of seabirds and revived the marine life around it. Local fishermen helped design the marine protected area, including the UK's first no-take zone, and the island now supports wildlife, fishing and visitors together.

items.title: Mrs. Moreau's Warbler: Stephen Moss on how birds got their names
items.why: Every birder eventually wonders who all these people in the field guide were and why a perfectly good warbler is named after somebody's wife. Stephen Moss wrote a whole book about it, and 10,000 Birds has dusted off its review. Good reading for anyone who has ever had to explain a megapode named after an explorer.
items.summary: A review, republished from the 10,000 Birds archive, of Stephen Moss's book on the origins of bird names. The reviewer finds it takes a different approach from earlier books on the subject, looking at the people, places and habits behind the names birds carry.

items.title: A website keeps Boston's lost bars open, at least in memory
items.why: Every city has bars that live on mainly in the arguments of people who drank there. Someone in Boston has given them a permanent home on the web, which is a public service of sorts. Expect a lot of 'wait, that's where that was'.
items.summary: Universal Hub points to a website devoted to remembering Boston bars that have closed for good, an online memorial for the city's vanished watering holes.

items.title: Split-level I/O scheduling: hooking the system call, page cache and block layers at once, via The Morning Paper
